synopsis: ACARP appears in two distinct validation strands: the Mining3-associated C26028 framework, dated January 2021, is a shared physical-test protocol that checks object detection before Level 8 or 9 intervention, whereas the UQ/ACARP simulator work studied proximity advisory and human interfaces rather than automatic braking [f16088, f11752, f573]. The physical framework uses limited choreographed Tier 2 scenarios and omits pre-existing site controls and complex dynamic vehicle interactions; for a team starting in October 2026, preparing an ACARP-style physical-test package is considered realistic by mid-2027 [f958, f803, f851]. The simulator research concerned Australian open-cut coal operations during 2017–2019, although the accessible project page lacks a clear publication date [f3465, f574]. A richer schematic interface reduced collision risk, braking force and travel time, but benefits were smaller with fewer experienced drivers, warning against a single generic operator model [f3466, f3467, f3470]. This is the strongest haul-truck-specific human-interface-loop evidence found, yet public material does not establish real-world operator-response fidelity, and an acceptable false-alarm rate remains unresolved [f3468, f3469, f3605].
